intro.title: The Night Journey
intro.lead: Late in the Makkan years, sorrow gathered around the Prophet ﷺ. Khadijah, who had sheltered his heart, died; Abu Talib, who had sheltered his life, died; and Ta’if answered his message with stones. It was after this season of grief, in the year the sira calls the Year of Sorrow, that Allah carried His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque and raised him through the seven heavens, brought nearer than any created being had been brought, and returned him before dawn carrying the gift his people still hold: the prayer.

anchor.text: The Isra itself, Masjid al-Haram to Masjid al-Aqsa, is stated by the Qur'an

chapters.title: The Year of Sorrow
chapters.body: Before the ascent came the breaking. Within a short span the Prophet ﷺ lost Khadijah, the first believer, the wife who had wrapped him in his trembling and spent her wealth on his mission, and Abu Talib, the uncle whose standing had held Quraysh away from him. When he walked to Ta’if seeking shelter for the message, its people set their fools on him until his sandals ran with blood. The sira remembers it as the Year of Sorrow. Heaven answered that grief not with ease but with nearness. What follows is the night on which the wounded servant was summoned upward, honored in the company of every prophet, and drawn closer than any created being had ever been drawn.
chapters.note: The name Year of Sorrow and the placing of the Night Journey soon after it rest on sira chronology; no authentic hadith fixes the exact year or calendar date, and any precise date given for this night is later convention, not transmission.

chapters.title: The Chest Was Opened
chapters.body: The narrations of Anas ibn Malik and Malik ibn Sa’sa’ah open quietly: the Prophet ﷺ lay resting near the House, in the state between sleeping and waking, when Jibril alayhis-salam descended to him. His chest was opened from the pit of the throat to the abdomen, and his heart was taken out and washed with the water of Zamzam. There was no violence in it; this was purification, the preparation of a vessel rather than a wound. A servant was about to be carried where nothing of earth could go with him. Before the body was raised through the heavens, the heart was made ready to bear what the heavens would show it, and to carry back down what it would be given.
chapters.note: An authentic narration in Sahih Muslim records an earlier opening of his chest in childhood; scholars read the washing on this night as a preparation specific to the ascent.

chapters.title: The Vessel of Wisdom and Faith
chapters.body: Then a basin of gold was brought, filled with wisdom and faith, and it was emptied into his chest before the chest was closed. The narrators do not explain how faith can fill a vessel, and the Prophet ﷺ did not elaborate; the report is left in its strangeness, as revelation sometimes is. What the night would ask of him was not courage alone but certainty, the settled knowledge that what the eye was about to see was true and from his Lord. Wisdom and faith were poured into him the way provision is given to a traveler, measured for the road ahead: seven heavens, the prophets in their stations, the Lote Tree at the limit of things, and words spoken beyond it.

chapters.title: The Arrival of al-Buraq
chapters.body: He was brought a mount whom the narrations call al-Buraq: a white beast, smaller than a mule and larger than a donkey, placing its hoof at the farthest point its sight could reach. The authentic reports say nothing more of its form, and restraint honors them; whatever later storytelling added belongs to imagination, not transmission. Distance, for such a creature, was a matter of glances. The Prophet ﷺ mounted, with Jibril beside him, and the road to Jerusalem shrank beneath that stride. In the narration of Anas he tied al-Buraq at the ring by the gate of the sanctuary, the same ring, he said, where the prophets before him had tied it, one small gesture binding this journey to every journey heaven had ever commanded.

chapters.title: From the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque
chapters.body: The Qur’an itself carries this stage of the journey, in words recited in every generation since: Glorified is He who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque, whose surroundings We have blessed, that We might show him of Our signs. Each word is weighed. It happened by night, in secrecy and stillness; he traveled as His servant, the title of deepest nearness; and the road ran first to al-Aqsa, sanctuary of the earlier prophets, before it turned upward. Makkah and Jerusalem were joined in a single night, and this ummah has understood ever since that its story does not begin with itself. The Prophet ﷺ entered a line of prophecy older than empires, and prayed where his brothers had prayed.
chapters.note: The majority of scholars hold the journey took place with body and soul together, awake, which is why Quraysh found the claim so enormous; a minority of early voices spoke of vision, and the commentaries record the discussion.

chapters.title: The Prayer of the Prophets
chapters.body: At Bayt al-Maqdis he entered the sanctuary and prayed two rak’ahs. In the narration of Abu Hurayrah, the time of prayer came and he led them, the assembled company of prophets gathered in rows behind one imam from the descendants of Isma’il alayhis-salam. The reports linger on no ceremony; the scene is given in a line, as if its meaning needed no help. Every messenger had carried the one call through his own people and his own age; on this night the callers themselves stood shoulder to shoulder, and the Prophet ﷺ of the final nation stood in front. Leadership in prayer is the quietest of honors, and it was granted quietly, in the sanctuary that had held prophecy for centuries.
chapters.note: Scholars differ over whether this congregational prayer occurred before the ascent or after the return; the transmitted wordings admit both arrangements.

chapters.title: The Choice Between Milk and Wine
chapters.body: Two vessels were set before him, one of milk and one of wine. He took the milk, and Jibril said: praise be to Allah who guided you to the fitrah; had you taken the wine, your ummah would have gone astray. The test was placed at the hinge of the journey, before the heavens opened. Milk is the first food of every human life, nourishment without confusion, sweetness that clarifies; wine is sweetness that unseats the mind. The choice was made once, on behalf of everyone who would afterward belong to him. In the Prophet’s ﷺ steady hand reaching for the plainer cup, the temper of the final religion was quietly fixed: a way aligned with how human beings are made.
chapters.note: Bukhari 3887 places offered vessels, wine, milk, and in some wordings honey, at Sidrat al-Muntaha, while Bukhari 5576 sets two vessels at Bayt al-Maqdis; scholars allow that both offerings occurred.

chapters.title: The First Gate of Heaven
chapters.body: Then the ascent, the Mi’raj, began. At the lowest heaven Jibril asked for the gate to be opened, and a voice asked: who is this? Jibril. And who is with you? Muhammad ﷺ. Has he been sent for? He has. Then the gate was opened, and the keeper said: welcome to him, and what an excellent coming is his. The exchange repeats at every heaven, and the narrations preserve it each time without shortening it, seven questions and seven welcomes. Heaven does not open by right of arrival but by invitation; even the best of creation entered as one sent for. Above the first gate the unseen world stood arranged in its ranks, waiting to receive its guest.

chapters.title: Adam and the Two Directions of Humanity
chapters.body: In the first heaven sat Adam alayhis-salam, the father of humankind. He greeted the Prophet ﷺ as a righteous son and a righteous prophet. In the narration of Abu Dharr, multitudes of souls were arrayed on his right and on his left; when he looked to his right he smiled, and when he looked to his left he wept. These were the souls of his descendants: the people of Paradise on the one hand, the people of the Fire on the other. The first ancestor still watches the long procession of his children, rejoicing and grieving by turns. No scene in the ascent is more human than this. The journey through the heavens begins with a father’s face, moved by what becomes of his family.

chapters.title: Yahya and Isa
chapters.body: In the second heaven he met the two maternal cousins, Yahya alayhis-salam and Isa alayhis-salam, son of Zakariyya alayhis-salam and son of Maryam. Each welcomed him as a righteous brother and a righteous prophet. The narrations pause on nothing further, yet the pairing carries weight of its own: two prophets of the house of Imran, one slain unjustly, one denied and then raised beyond reach, now standing together in peace above the world that refused them. For the Prophet ﷺ, walking out of his own years of rejection, the second heaven held a quiet reassurance. Those wronged for the sake of the message do not end inside the wrong done to them; they end in welcome, in company, in light.

chapters.title: Yusuf and Beauty
chapters.body: In the third heaven stood Yusuf alayhis-salam. In the narration of Anas the Prophet ﷺ said of him: he had been given half of all beauty. The line is spoken plainly, without envy and without explanation. Yusuf’s beauty had once been his trial, the cause of the pit, the caravan, and the prison; here it stands transfigured, a mark of honor in a station of honor. The tradition understands his portion as half of beauty itself, and understands too that the fairest of faces was matched by the purest patience. He welcomed the Prophet ﷺ as a brother and a prophet and prayed for his good. What the world once sold at a low price, heaven displays at its true worth.

chapters.title: Idris and the High Station
chapters.body: In the fourth heaven he met Idris alayhis-salam, and the narration itself reaches for the Qur’an to describe him: We raised him to a high station. Little is transmitted of Idris beyond truthfulness and prophethood, and the ascent adds no legend to him; it simply shows the verse fulfilled, a man raised, in the plainest sense, into the heights. There is a lesson in the economy of it. Some of Allah’s servants are known through volumes; some are summarized in a single verse and a single greeting. Idris welcomed the Prophet ﷺ as the others had, righteous brother, righteous prophet, and the travelers passed on upward, through a station whose name the Qur’an had given before the night confirmed it.
chapters.note: Some transmissions vary which heaven a given prophet occupies; this sequence follows the narration of Malik ibn Sa’sa’ah shared by Bukhari and Muslim.

chapters.title: Harun
chapters.body: In the fifth heaven was Harun alayhis-salam, brother of Musa alayhis-salam and the voice that had steadied a nation while its deliverer stood on the mountain. He greeted the Prophet ﷺ with the words of welcome the others had used, a righteous brother and a righteous prophet. The narrations grant him no speech beyond the greeting, and the silence suits him; his whole prophethood had been a ministry of support, eloquence placed in the service of another man’s mission. In the ordering of the heavens he stands one level beneath his brother, near him beyond the world as he was within it. For a Prophet ﷺ who would soon lean hard on Musa’s counsel, meeting the helper just before the counselor carries its own gentle fitness.

chapters.title: Musa
chapters.body: In the sixth heaven he met Musa, and here the narration slows. When the Prophet ﷺ moved past him toward the seventh heaven, Musa wept. Asked why, he answered: I weep because a young man was sent after me whose ummah will enter Paradise in greater numbers than mine. The scholars read those tears with care: not envy, which has no life in that world, but the sorrow of a shepherd who wanted more for his own flock. Musa had carried Banu Isra’il through sea, desert, and forty years of wandering, and he loved them still. His weeping honors both nations at once. No one in the heavens will engage the Prophet ﷺ more than Musa, and the tears are only the first sign of his care.

chapters.title: Ibrahim and the Frequented House
chapters.body: In the seventh heaven, nearest the boundary of created things, he found Ibrahim alayhis-salam, the intimate friend of Allah, reclining against al-Bayt al-Ma’mur, the Frequented House. Ibrahim greeted him as a righteous son and a righteous prophet, the words Adam had spoken at the first heaven, so that the ascent is framed by two fathers: the father of humankind at its floor, the father of prophets at its summit. The House he leaned against stands above the heavens as the Ka’bah stands upon the earth, one axis of worship running through all the worlds. The man who had raised the foundations of the earthly House now rests beside its heavenly likeness, and between the two Houses the whole religion is strung like a single thread.

chapters.title: The Seventy Thousand Who Never Return
chapters.body: Of al-Bayt al-Ma’mur he was told: every day seventy thousand angels enter it, and those who leave never return to it; it is the last they will ever see of it. The number is not ornament, it is a window onto the scale of the unseen. Creation is vaster than any census, and its worship never repeats. Every day a new host, every day a farewell, from before Adam until the ending of days, and no angel comes twice. On earth, worshippers circle the Ka’bah and come back year after year; the heavens are so thick with servants that a single visit is a lifetime’s share. The report leaves the mind at the edge of a number it cannot see over, which is where minds belong before the unseen.

chapters.title: Sidrat al-Muntaha
chapters.body: Then he was raised to Sidrat al-Muntaha, the Lote Tree of the farthest limit, which the Qur’an names as the station of a second encounter with revelation. The narration reaches for the largest familiar things to describe it: fruits like the great jars of Hajar, leaves like the ears of elephants. From its base issued four rivers, two hidden and two apparent; the hidden pair, he was told, are rivers of Paradise, and the apparent pair are named as the Nile and the Euphrates. Here the knowledge of every created being finds its ceiling; what rises from below ends at this tree, and what descends from above is received at it. Then it was covered by that which covered it, and it changed, until none of Allah’s creation could have described its beauty.
chapters.note: Commentators, an-Nawawi among them, read the naming of the Nile and the Euphrates as a statement of the blessing attached to their lands rather than a map of their springs.

chapters.title: What No Created Tongue Can Describe
chapters.body: What happened at the summit is guarded by the Qur’an’s own reticence: the heart did not lie about what it saw; the sight neither swerved nor overreached. Here the first generations themselves differed, and honesty requires saying so. Aisha, the Mother of the Believers, held that whoever claims the Prophet ﷺ saw his Lord has erred gravely; what he saw in his true form was Jibril, and the verses of an-Najm describe that vision. Ibn Abbas held that he saw Him, and in one wording, saw Him with his heart, twice. Later scholars often joined the two: a vision of the heart affirmed, a vision of the eyes denied, and the essence of Allah unseen by anyone in this life. The summit of the ascent stays, fittingly, beyond created description.
chapters.note: Both positions are preserved in Sahih Muslim; the disagreement concerns the vision at the summit, never the reality of the ascent itself.

chapters.title: Paradise and Kawthar
chapters.body: He was shown Paradise. The narration of Malik ibn Sa’sa’ah gives two details and stops: domes of pearl, and soil of musk. In another authentic report the Prophet ﷺ said: while I was walking in Paradise I came upon a river whose banks were vaults of hollowed pearl, and I asked Jibril, what is this? He said: this is al-Kawthar, which your Lord has given you. The shortest surah of the Qur’an had promised that abundance in a single breath; the night showed it flowing. The descriptions end early, and rightly. Of the home of the righteous we are handed the scent of its earth, the curve of one riverbank, and the certainty that it is real, prepared, and waiting.

chapters.title: Warnings Shown in the Unseen
chapters.body: The journey also carried warnings. The strongest of these reports concerns the backbiters: the Prophet ﷺ passed a people with nails of copper, tearing at their own faces and chests, and was told: these are the ones who ate the flesh of people and assaulted their honor. Abu Dawud transmits it with a sound chain. Other punishment scenes in circulation, the devourers of usury, the neglecters of prayer, and more, rest on narrations of varying strength, and several belong to a separate, authentic dream of the Prophet ﷺ rather than to this night; popular retellings have braided the two together. Precision here is itself reverence. What stands firm is the emphasis: on the night of nearness, sins of the tongue against absent people were singled out for horror.
chapters.note: The backbiters scene is Abu Dawud 4878 and is graded strong; several widely retold scenes come instead from the separate dream narration in Bukhari 7047 or from weak chains, and each must be weighed on its own.

chapters.title: Fifty Prayers
chapters.body: Above the Lote Tree the obligation was given: fifty prayers in every day and night. The Prophet ﷺ accepted and turned homeward. There was no bargaining at the summit; the servant received what his Lord ordained, and the number itself declared how much of a human life is owed to remembrance. Fifty prayers would have threaded worship through every waking hour, a life with no seam between devotion and the rest. That, in truth, is the scale of the debt. What follows in the story is not a lightening of that truth but a mercy in its accounting, and like every mercy of this night it arrives through love: the love of an old prophet for a nation he had never met.

chapters.title: The Counsel of Musa
chapters.body: Descending, he passed Musa, who asked: what were you commanded? Fifty prayers each day, he said. Musa answered: your ummah will not manage it; I tried people before you, and I treated Banu Isra’il with the hardest treatment; return to your Lord and ask Him to lighten it for your ummah. So the Prophet ﷺ returned, and a portion was removed. Musa sent him back, and back again, the narration patient with every repetition, until five remained. The scene honors both men: the elder prophet spending his hard experience on a nation not his own, and the final Prophet ﷺ unashamed to stand before his Lord again and again as a pleader for his people. Between Musa’s realism and Muhammad’s ﷺ asking, the shape of the ummah’s day was settled.
chapters.note: The narrations differ on whether the reductions came ten at a time or five at a time; the endpoint of five is agreed upon in every sound wording.

chapters.title: Five Prayers with the Reward of Fifty
chapters.body: When five remained, Musa urged him to ask once more. The Prophet ﷺ answered: I have asked my Lord until I am shy before Him; I am content, and I submit. Then a caller announced: I have carried through My obligation and lightened the burden on My servants; they are five, and they are fifty; the word is not changed with Me. Five in performance, fifty in reward, each prayer weighed at ten, the arithmetic of a generosity that had intended mercy from the first. The final number was not wrung from heaven; it was a gift heaven had prepared, given in a way that let one prophet counsel, another plead, and a people know forever how they were loved. He came down carrying the religion’s daily heartbeat.

chapters.title: The Return Before Dawn
chapters.body: He was returned to Makkah before dawn had broken over it, the whole immensity folded into a fraction of one night. The authentic narrations spend no words on the homeward road; a journey that outran description outran its narrators too. Morning found the Prophet ﷺ among his people carrying the heaviest of tidings: that he had been, in a single night, to Jerusalem and beyond the seventh heaven. The sira adds that he spoke of caravans passed on the way and the hour of their arrival, details his hearers could test; those reports vary in strength and are read as supporting detail, not foundation. The foundation was starker: one truthful man’s word against the whole weight of the possible.

chapters.title: The Test of Al-Aqsa
chapters.body: By morning the claim was in the open, and Quraysh received it as a gift, the perfect absurdity with which to finish him. Men who had ridden a month to reach Syria knew what one night meant. Those who had seen Jerusalem pressed him to describe it. The Prophet ﷺ later told what happened: when Quraysh called me a liar, I stood in al-Hijr, and Allah displayed Bayt al-Maqdis before me, and I began to tell them of its signs while I was looking at it. He had crossed it by night, his gaze set on higher things; the examiners wanted its doors and windows. So the sanctuary was raised before his eyes, and he answered from the original. The test built to break the story became part of its proof.

chapters.title: Abu Bakr As-Siddiq
chapters.body: The report reached Abu Bakr as a taunt: your companion claims he went by night to Bayt al-Maqdis and returned before morning. His answer, preserved in the report of al-Hakim and others, wasted no breath on geography: if he said it, then he has spoken the truth. And he went further: I believe him in what is more distant than that; I believe him about news from heaven arriving in a morning or an evening. From that day, the tradition holds, he was called as-Siddiq, the ever-affirming. The grading of the naming report is discussed by the scholars, and its meaning is beyond dispute in the memory of the ummah. Faith of this kind does not verify claims one by one; it has already verified the man.
chapters.note: The naming report is in al-Hakim’s Mustadrak, graded sahih by him with adh-Dhahabi concurring; it is not in Bukhari or Muslim, though the disbelief of Quraysh that occasioned it is.

chapters.title: The Gift Carried by Every Muslim
chapters.body: Every other ordinance came down to the earth; the prayer alone was given at the summit, received without any intermediary space between the Giver and the one receiving. That is its measure. In the narration of Ibn Mas’ud, three things were given that night: the five prayers, the closing verses of Surat al-Baqarah, and the promise of forgiveness for whoever meets Allah without associating anything with Him. Of the whole journey, the heavens, the Tree, the rivers, the welcomes, this is what the Prophet ﷺ carried home. Fourteen centuries on, a tired worker rising before first light to pray fajr is holding the night’s gift. Five times a day, in every land on earth, some part of this night returns: a believer turns toward the qiblah, and the road opened in the Year of Sorrow opens again.
